headline: AI-powered Quenya TTS improved with Tolkien's own voice
summary: Researchers enhanced a text-to-speech system for Tolkien's Quenya language by refining pronunciation rules and comparing output to recordings of Tolkien himself.
details: A master's thesis project, QuenyaTTS, has been significantly improved by analyzing pronunciation rules from Tolkien's linguistic notes and comparing the synthesized speech to recordings of Tolkien reciting 'Namárië'. The goal was to enhance the accuracy and naturalness of the Quenya text-to-speech system.

The project involved meticulous rule refinement for Quenya phonetics, cross-referencing with various linguistic sources including Tolkien's own notes. Key pronunciation aspects like 'hr' and 'hl' sounds, the 'w' to 'v' conversion, archaic spellings, and syllable stress were adjusted to align with established rules and Tolkien's likely pronunciation.

To assess the improvements, a script was developed to compare the QuenyaTTS output line-by-line with an audio recording of Tolkien reciting 'Namárië'. While the recognizer isn't perfect and Tolkien's tape is old, the comparison provided valuable insights into the TTS system's accuracy and highlighted areas for further refinement.

Initial comparisons showed that where the recognizer could clearly identify Tolkien's speech, it aligned with the refined rules. A notable difference emerged in the 'ly' sound, where the rules suggest a single phoneme but Tolkien's voice seemed to contain two. The project opted to retain the single sound as sources leave both readings open.

The project also addressed technical issues, such as clipping at the beginning of synthesized speech, by adding a silent pause. Efforts were made to isolate the Quenya-specific components of the TTS system, ensuring the underlying Toucan engine remained unchanged and its Finnish borrowing settings were maintained.

Attempts to fine-tune the model with limited Quenya recordings led to overfitting, demonstrating that better rules are crucial. The project is now focused on gathering more extensive, high-quality Quenya speech data, including recordings from the author and a call for volunteers to contribute their voices.

headline_marked: Meta's Muse AI [[now lets US users video chat]] with animated avatars
headline: Meta's Muse AI now lets US users video chat with animated avatars
summary: The AI agent, nicknamed Jolly, can be customized and uses subtle expressions to match conversation tone, with video chat available on mobile, web, and Mac.
details: Meta has officially rolled out its Muse Voice feature, allowing users in the U.S. to video chat with its consumer AI agent, Muse. This feature, first previewed in September, utilizes new AI models for real-time avatar and voice technology.

Unlike other AI competitors that offer voice chat, Meta's Muse features a customizable animated avatar named Jolly. Users can personalize the avatar to resemble a person, animal, or any other character, aiming to foster a stronger connection with the AI.

The Muse avatar is designed to engage users with subtle expressions and gestures that align with the conversation's tone. This anthropomorphic approach is intended to make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent.

A demo video showcased Meta's Chief AI Officer, Alexandr Wang, interacting with his dog-like Muse avatar. The conversation included lighthearted banter about memes, with the AI suggesting disclaimers for potentially misinterpreted posts.

This expansion into video and voice chat comes as Meta prepares to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for Muse later this year. The device will feature the AI avatar on a small screen, enabling conversations and task execution.
Real-time conversations with Muse are currently supported on mobile, web, and Mac platforms. Future integrations are planned for Meta's AI Glasses and the upcoming 'Muse Charm' hardware.
